title: 5 forearm extensors Mistakes That Are Destroying Your extensor tendons
description: Everyone trains the squeeze. Almost nobody trains the opening, and your extensor tendons pay for the imbalance. Here is the finger spread test that exposes it, the five mistakes behind weak extensors, and the balance work that protects your elbows and completes your grip.

scenes.narration: Here is a test almost nobody passes the first time. Loop a rubber band around all five fingertips of one hand, thumb included. Now spread your fingers WIDE against the band, fully open, and close them again. Count how many full spreads you can do in thirty seconds before the opening turns weak and sloppy. That is your spread number. It feels like a party trick until rep fifteen, when a system you have never trained starts burning in the back of your forearm. Keep the number. At the end, I will show you the five mistakes that keep this system weak, and why it quietly decides the health of your elbows.

scenes.label: THE THIRTY-SPREAD LINE
scenes.narration: Here is the line. Thirty full spreads in thirty seconds, clean and wide, against a band with real tension. Under fifteen, your opening system is basically ASLEEP, which is normal, because almost no training program on earth touches it. Fifteen to twenty-four, the extensors are waking up but they fade fast. Twenty-five to twenty-nine, you are balanced, front and back of the forearm sharing the work. Thirty clean spreads: your openers are WIRED, and your grip closes harder because of it. A hand is only as strong as the system that can also open it.

Look at the back of the forearm on this plate. Running down it are the EXTENSOR tendons, the cables that open your hand, straighten your fingers and stabilise your wrist against every grip you make. When you crush a bar, the flexors in the front do the squeezing, but the extensors in the back fire at the same time to keep the wrist from folding. They are the brakes and the steering on every grip you own. And here is the problem: nearly every exercise you have ever done trains the front. The back gets nothing but leftovers, year after year, until the imbalance starts talking to your elbow. The anatomy has one more layer worth knowing. The extensors do not just open the fingers; the wrist extensors, running to the back of the hand, hold your wrist in the strong, slightly cocked position every powerful grip depends on. Do a push-up on your fists or hold a heavy bag and they are working as hard as the flexors, silently. When they fatigue, the wrist sags into flexion, the flexors lose their best length, and crush force falls off a cliff. Weak extensors do not just unbalance the forearm. They tax every grip you make from the top down.

beats.title: BRAKES AND STEERING
lines: Extensors stabilise the wrist on every grip.
They fire even when you only squeeze.

scenes.narration: The balance matters more than the size. Studies of grip and forearm pain keep landing on the same finding: people with stubborn outer-elbow pain, the classic tennis elbow pattern, almost always show weak, easily fatigued extensors on the sore side. The flexors overpower the extensors on every grip, the wrist wobbles under load, and the extensor tendons absorb stress they were never built to take alone. Strengthen the opening system and two things happen. Your wrist locks straight under heavy grips, so your crushing force goes UP. And the tendon at your elbow finally gets a partner instead of a bully. The modern world makes this worse in a specific way. Hours of mouse and keyboard work hold the extensors in a low, endless contraction, too light to train them and too constant to rest them. Desk workers often test terribly on the spread test despite never missing the gym, because their opening system is not weak from neglect alone; it is tired from overtime. If that is you, the fix is the same work, gentler: light bands, full range, spread through the day. You are not just building the system. You are paying off its debt.

There is a performance secret hiding here too. Between reps of any grip work, your hand must open fully and fast to reset. Climbers call it the shake-out, and the speed of that reset is pure extensor work. Weak openers mean slow resets, and slow resets mean your next grip starts at ninety percent, then eighty, then seventy. Across a long hang or a heavy carry, the guy with trained extensors is not stronger on rep one. He is stronger on rep thirty, because his hand still opens all the way and closes all the way, every single time.

beats.title: STRONG ON REP THIRTY
lines: Full opening means a full next grip.
Weak openers leak force rep by rep.

scenes.narration: Try one thing right now to feel the system work. Make a tight fist and squeeze hard. Now, keeping the fist closed, cock your wrist backward. Feel the top of the forearm light up? That is the extensor mass, switching on to stabilise. Now let the wrist flop forward and squeeze again. The grip feels hollow, because it is: the flexors lost their anchor. Every strong grip you have ever made was a duet, and the partner you never trained has been carrying half the performance. The spread test is simply the first time anyone asked the partner to perform alone.

beats.title: THE ANCHOR TEST
lines: Wrist back: the grip feels solid.
Wrist flopped: the grip feels hollow.

scenes.narration: Your skinny advantage here is sneaky. Extensor work is low-load by nature, bands and spreads, so it needs almost no recovery and can be trained daily, even on rest days, even at a desk. Bigger guys ignore this work because it looks like nothing, and their imbalances grow with their forearms. You can build the most balanced forearms in the gym with a rubber band and five spare minutes a day, and nobody will even know you are training. The best cable work is the work nobody sees.
Spread with me. Thirty seconds of full, clean spreads against the band, thirty seconds rest, four rounds. Slow enough to open all the way, every rep. Go.

Now the five mistakes. Mistake one: never training the opening at all. A forearm built on one side is a cable system with half its wires missing. Mistake two: SNAPPING the band. Fast, jerky spreads teach nothing. The tendon wants slow, full-range tension, open to a full stretch and close under control. Mistake three: using a band so light it feels like air, forever. Progress the band like any other load. Mistake four: training through a growing ache on the outer elbow. That ache is information, and pushing through it is how small irritation becomes a long layoff. If elbow pain persists, see a professional and get it assessed properly. Mistake five: only training spreads when you remember, once a month. Extensors respond to frequency. A few clean minutes daily beats a heroic session every few weeks.

So, your spread number. Under fifteen: your opening system is asleep, and waking it is the cheapest upgrade left in your forearms. Fifteen to twenty-four: BUILDING, the balance is coming. Twenty-five to twenty-nine: balanced and genuinely rare. Thirty clean spreads: WIRED openers, and your elbows will thank you for decades. Put your number in the comments, just the reps. In thirty days we spread against the band again, and the back of your forearm will have a score of its own to brag about.

Thirty days of quiet band work, and the test will show a system the mirror still cannot see. Subscribe, because every week we test another cable most people never train. This is {channel}. Train the cable.
